title: Forgiveness and health
hookLine: studies link forgiving with lower stress, though cause and effect are unclear

lines: A MERRY HEART, LIKE A MEDICINE.
A HUNCH ABOUT HEART AND BODY.
cards: A line from the book of Proverbs: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones." Whoever wrote it had a hunch that what happens in the heart shows up in the body, down to the bones.
Researchers now test hunches like that with questionnaires, heart monitors and blood pressure readings, and some of them have pointed those tools at forgiveness. What they found is worth hearing.
So is what they're careful not to claim.

teach.b: In the research gathered in the book Forgiveness and Health, edited by Loren Toussaint, Everett Worthington and David Williams, people who forgive more readily tend to report less stress.
Forgiving and lower stress show up together. Now the honest catch, and it's a big one. Showing up together is not the same as one causing the other.
Maybe forgiving lowers stress. Maybe people who are already less stressed find it easier to forgive. Maybe something else, like good sleep or good friends, helps both at once.
The researchers themselves say the direction isn't settled, and anyone who promises that forgiving will fix your blood pressure is saying more than the studies do.
A closer look at one moment: the psychologist Charlotte Witvliet asked people to bring to mind someone who had hurt them, and then to spend time either rehearsing the grudge or imagining forgiving.
While they rehearsed the grudge, their bodies showed more signs of stress: heart rate and blood pressure went up. While they imagined forgiving, those signs were lower.
That's a small window, measured in minutes, not a lifetime. But it shows a grudge isn't only a thought. The body takes part.
So what do you do with a link you can't fully explain? Not treat forgiveness like a pill.

teach.h: NOT A PILL, SOMETHING TO NOTICE.
teach.b: Treat it as something to notice: what holding does in your own shoulders, and what letting go does.

teach.h: A MERRY HEART DOETH GOOD LIKE A MEDICINE.
teach.b: The Proverbs writer never ran a study. The hunch was about bones.

how: Researchers study forgiveness and health with questionnaires and body measures such as heart rate and blood pressure; they report links between forgiving and lower stress while saying cause and effect are not settled.

games.q: a study finds that people who forgive more also report less stress. what can you fairly conclude?
o: the two go together, but which causes which is unclear.
games.why: together is not cause. forgiving might lower stress, lower stress might make forgiving easier, or something else might help both. the researchers say the direction isn't settled.

practice: Hold one small grievance, nothing heavy, for a few breaths, and check in with the body: the jaw, the shoulders, the hands, the breath itself.
Then try letting it go, even only for the length of this sit, and check in again; there's no right result, and whatever you find, or don't, is worth knowing.

wordCard.voice: Witvliet. The psychologist whose study found the body's stress signs rose during a rehearsed grudge, and fell while imagining forgiving. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: lighter. Not a cure, just something worth noticing in your own body. See you tomorrow.
